title: Psychiatric nurse neglected patient who took own life

input.lead: Laurence Tchapong failed to carry out required observations and falsified records
input.summary: Laurence Tchapong failed to carry out required observations and falsified records
input.evidence_text: Psychiatric nurse neglected patient who took own life - BBC News Image source, Merseyside Police Image caption, Tchapong was found guilty of wilful neglect By Haider Saleem Reporting from North West Published 1 September 2026 A mental health nurse who failed to check on a patient she had a "grudge" against before she took her own life has been jailed for four years. Laurence Tchapong, 54, was required to check Amy Barber, 22, every five minutes at the Brooklands psychiatric intensive care unit at Clatterbridge Hospital in Wirral, but Liverpool Crown Court heard Tchapong completed records suggesting checks had taken place on 30 June 2022. Amy was found unresponsive by a colleague but could not be saved, and CCTV showed Tchapong had not checked on her for 25 minutes. Tchapong, from Manchester, denied wilful neglect but was convicted following a trial. Image caption, Amy Barber was described as "the most caring, bright, funny girl" The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said Amy Barber had a complex mental health history, had been detained under the Mental Health Act and had previously displayed significant self-harming behaviour. Sentencing, Judge Murray said Tchapong had "deliberately lied" in the observation records in an attempt to evade justice. The judge said Tchapong had previously been given a verbal warning after Amy Barber photographed her sleeping and reported her to management. He said: "I am sure the defendant held a grudge against Amy for a perceived lack of warmth towards the defendant, and because Amy had previously complained about the defendant." title: Inquest to be held nearly nine years after Walkden arson murders

input.lead: Michelle Pearson and her four children were all killed following a petrol bomb attack at their home
input.summary: Michelle Pearson and her four children were all killed following a petrol bomb attack at their home
input.evidence_text: Inquest to be held nearly nine years after Walkden arson murders - BBC News Image source, Family handout Image caption, Michelle Pearson, 37, and her four children were all killed following the petrol bomb attack Published 1 September 2026 An inquest is to be held into the deaths of a mother and her four children murdered in an arson attack almost nine years on from the incident. The blaze in December 2017 claimed the lives of Demi Pearson, 15, her brother Brandon, eight, and sisters Lacie, seven, and Lia, three. Their mother, Michelle Pearson, suffered 68% burns to her body and "clung on to life" until she died, aged 37, on 25 August, 2019 – 20 months after the attack in Walkden, Greater Manchester. Timothy Brennand, senior coroner for Manchester West, has set a date of 5 October for the inquest to begin. Relatives of the family believe their deaths were "wholly preventable", and have raised the question of "missed opportunities" to protect them by state agencies. Michelle Pearson had "begged" to be rehoused and called police on five occasions in the two weeks before the fatal attack, the trial of her killers heard. Zak Bolland and David Worrall were jailed for life for the attack in 2018. After a series of delays following the trial, Brennand set the inquest date in a brief hearing at Bolton Coroners' Court. The hearing was told the inquest is scheduled to last up to two months with seven police officers individually represented, along with their force Greater Manchester Police (GMP), Salford City Council, two hospital trusts, Wigan Council, Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service and the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC). Image source, Police handout Image caption, Zak Bolland (left) and David Worrall were found guilty of the murders of Michelle Pearson

title: Four more people face arson charge over moorland fire

input.lead: The wildfire at Dove Stone reservoir near Greenfield, Oldham, took more than three weeks to put out
input.summary: The wildfire at Dove Stone reservoir near Greenfield, Oldham, took more than three weeks to put out
input.evidence_text: Four more people have been charged with arson in connection with a wildfire The blaze at Dove Stone reservoir, near Greenfield, Saddleworth, Greater Manchester, broke out on 11 July and was declared a major incident by the fire service. It took more than three weeks to extinguish Tyler Warburton, 18, Toby Wilde, 18, Jake Eyre, 19, and Lyreec Bryan-Gavin, 22, are all accused of arson with recklessness as to whether life was endangered and have all been bailed ahead of their scheduled court appearance in February at Manchester Magistrates' Court Shania Care-Slede has also been charged with arson offences, which she has denied and is to go on trial over in May Wilde and Eyre are also charged with possession of class B drugs (cannabis) The reservoir was reopened to the public for the first time on 27 August

title: Rochdale campers urged not to feed horses dangerous foods

input.lead: Horses in Rochdale have been given chicken bones, red onions, and lemons
input.summary: Horses in Rochdale have been given chicken bones, red onions, and lemons
input.evidence_text: Rochdale campers urged not to feed horses dangerous foods - BBC News Image source, Rachel Image caption, This photo was posted on Facebook to help find the collapsed horse's owner By Jade Taylorson North West Published 1 September 2026 A horse nearly died after being fed dangerous foods by campers near a farm, prompting a warning from the animal's owner. Julie Kershaw said people had been throwing unsuitable food into her field on Syke Moors in Rochdale over the summer, including chicken bones, red onions, and lemons. She is now warning people about the dangers after her horse, Frank, collapsed. "Just please don't do it because you're causing a lot of distress to the owners and the animals, and it's a lot of money – and if you can't get them right, then you've lost your pet," Julie said. Thirteen‑year-old Freya and her mother Rachel were out walking when they spotted the horse in trouble. "He just literally collapsed to the floor then went on to his side," Rachel told BBC Radio Manchester . "His breathing was really heavy and you could see his whole body shaking." Image source, Rachel Image caption, Freya has been around horses from a young age so knew how to comfort Frank Freya sat and comforted the animal before asking her mother to put an appeal on Facebook to help alert the owner. "I'm really proud of her. Within 10 minutes, Julie was on her way," Rachel said. Julie said she was "totally distressed" when she arrived. She said she was told by a vet that her horse had colitis, an inflammation of the colon, which could have spread and been fatal. "It was the worst thing. He could actually have died," she said. Image caption, Julie thanked Freya for alerting her and for staying with Frank until she arrived Freya said she was relieved to hear the horse later recovered. "

title: Free buses for Greater Mancheser school children in temporary housing

input.lead: The move is another new policy announced by Greater Manchester mayor Bev Craig
input.summary: The move is another new policy announced by Greater Manchester mayor Bev Craig
input.evidence_text: Children living in temporary housing in Greater Manchester will get free bus travel to and from school on the city region's Bee Network from 1 September, mayor Bev Craig has announced The move is part of The Greater Manchester Strategy, a plan for the region's next decade which is focused on reducing the number of families and children in temporary accommodation It means children placed in temporary accommodation can always get to their school, maintaining their routine and minimising disruption to their education Families who are eligible, which includes those living more than two miles from their school or where their route is considered unsafe to walk, will be assessed for inclusion by their local council, which will then issue a pass Sam Pratt, policy and communications lead at the Shared Health Foundation, a charity that supports homeless families in Greater Manchester, said: "Families who are homelessness are struggling to pay bills, travel costs and other things while they are homeless "So actually, this new policy is absolutely ground-breaking to have extra support and extra wrap-around support for these families, and we believe that it's right to put children's education first"

The attraction, which ‘no one talks about’ locally, is already bringing in people from across the country Daisy Nook Country Park is a 40 hectare site in the River Medlock valley which sits in both Oldham and Tameside boroughs. Daisy Nook’s history stretches back over 200 years where the canals there acted as a key supplier of coal that powered Manchester’s industrial revolution and The area is known for its beautiful scenery, wildlife, and waterways and is popular with photographers. Later this month, the Friends of Daisy Nook Country Park are set to formally sign an agreement on September 11 to help move an ‘ambitious’ community led programme forward Working with the Hollinwood Canal Society, this will look to restore and regenerate the park. £120,000 of funds is set to be spent over the coming months which will help restore sections of the historic canal and a former boat pond This is on top of work since 2024 to improve paths, create community spaces, tackle invasive species like Japanese knotweed and Himalayan balsam, improve accessibility, and carry out repairs

input.evidence_text: Salford motion capture startup bought by listed firm Posted on September 1, 2026 by staff Salford motion capture startup bought by listed firm Oxford Metrics plc moves for Captive Devices, founded in 2024 by trio of former Epic Games engineers, in deal worth up to £750k Share: Founders MediaTech A Salford motion capture startup has been bought by Oxford Metrics plc. Captive Devices was founded in 2024 by a trio of former Epic Games engineers – including Fred Isaac (pictured) – and received support from GM Business Growth Hub’s Innovation Service in securing innovation grants . A developer of professional head-mounted camera systems and software, it enables markerless facial performance capture, used in visual effects, games and virtual production. Oxford Metrics is a smart sensing and measurement technology group serving life sciences, entertainment, engineering and manufacturing markets. The acquisition adds specialist facial capture to its platform Vicon, which has an established market leadership in body tracking. Captive Devices’ first product was CoreHMC, a head-mounted camera facial motion capture system. The technology captures real human facial expressions and translates them into digital animation data, without the cost or complexity typically associated with bespoke setups. Instead of complicated tailored camera rigs, with custom software builds, time-intensive installation and ongoing technical support, the Captive Devices concept works straight out of the box. Its founding team – who designed and built similar systems prior to founding the business – will be joining Vicon.
